# Calibration corpus, English (VER-07). Written for this project and quoted from nowhere, so the
# model cannot read a passage from memory: in the first mini run it read famous public-domain
# texts as it knew them, turning "a Jefferson of the United States" back into "a Congress", and
# the corruptions never reached the audio. Each passage has a name, a number and a clause, so
# every corruption type applies. One passage per line; the first 20 are the good candidates.
# Do not reorder: sample IDs, the split and the corruptions all derive from this file and the seed.
On the third morning of the thaw, Marguerite Ollander walked the eleven miles to Pellbridge with a basket of eggs and a letter she had never meant to send.
The ferry from Castlemore left at seven, but the captain, a quiet man named Ruddick, always waited for the baker's boy before he cast off.
In the spring of that year the council voted to rebuild the old granary, though only four of the nine members had ever seen it full.
Tobias Wren kept two ledgers, one for the shop and one for the debts nobody would admit to, and he trusted neither of them completely.
The orchard behind the Hallorans' house produced more pears than apples, which surprised everyone except the woman who had planted it.
When the bell at Saint Aldric's cracked in the frost, the village raised forty pounds in a week and argued about the new one for a year.
Edwina Marsh wrote to her brother every Sunday, and in thirty years of letters she never once mentioned the farm they had both left behind.
The road to Kettering Cross was long and badly drained, and in wet weather the carrier charged double for anything heavier than a sack of flour.
Six lamps were lit along the quay each evening, and the harbour master counted them twice because the first count was always wrong.
Professor Hale believed that every map was a kind of argument, and he made his students redraw the county from memory before they saw a real one.
The mill at Dunmere ran day and night through the autumn, and the miller's daughter learned to sleep through a noise that kept visitors awake.
After the flood, the families on Wexley Lane shared one kitchen for twelve days, and several of them later said it was the best month of their lives.
Arthur Bellamy sold the same clock three times, and each buyer returned it with the same complaint: it kept perfect time, but only in the dark.
The school at Fenwick had one teacher, twenty-two pupils and a stove that worked only when the wind came from the east.
By the time the telegram reached Lowenstead, the ship it described had already docked safely and its passengers had gone home for supper.
Constance Albery planted a hedge of holly along the northern wall, and for fifty winters it was the only green thing visible from the road.
The bridge at Carrow was built in nine months by a crew of thirty, and it is still standing, which is more than can be said for the crew's reputation.
Every new tenant of the corner house complained about the draught, and every one of them stayed longer than they had planned.
The market at Brindle opened at dawn on Thursdays, and by eight o'clock the best cheese had gone and the gossip had only just begun.
Henrietta Vale learned to sail at sixty, and she said the hardest part was not the knots but admitting she had been afraid of the water all along.
The library at Ashcombe lent books for two weeks, but the librarian, Mr Pryce, rarely asked for them back before the end of the season.
Three generations of the Tanner family fished the same stretch of river, and none of them ever agreed on the best hour to cast a line.
